Accounts with an opened date are in Sales.Customers (AccountOpenedDate). To get the earliest one, I order by that date ascending and take one row. I add CustomerID as a tiebreaker so the result is deterministic when several accounts share the same date.

```sql
SELECT CustomerName
FROM Sales.Customers
ORDER BY AccountOpenedDate ASC, CustomerID ASC
LIMIT 1;
```

Customers link to a city through DeliveryCityID, cities link to a state/province through StateProvinceID, and the state name comes from Application.StateProvinces. I'll join the three tables and count customers per state province name. I use the delivery city because it is the customer's primary location, and the Website.Customers view uses it too.

```sql
SELECT sp.StateProvinceName,
       COUNT(c.CustomerID) AS customer_count
FROM Sales.Customers AS c
JOIN Application.Cities AS ci ON c.DeliveryCityID = ci.CityID
JOIN Application.StateProvinces AS sp ON ci.StateProvinceID = sp.StateProvinceID
GROUP BY sp.StateProvinceName
ORDER BY customer_count DESC, sp.StateProvinceName;
```

The question is ambiguous. "Average transaction amount per customer" most naturally means grouping Sales.CustomerTransactions by customer and averaging TransactionAmount.

Steps:
1. Use Sales.CustomerTransactions, which holds the per-customer transactions.
2. Group by CustomerID.
3. Average TransactionAmount for each group.
4. Join to Sales.Customers to show the customer name.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID,
       c.CustomerName,
       AVG(ct.TransactionAmount) AS avg_transaction_amount
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions ct
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = ct.CustomerID
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
ORDER BY c.CustomerID;
```

"Completed successfully" most plausibly maps to `IsFinalized = true`, meaning the transaction is finalized. I used `Sales.CustomerTransactions`, since it holds the main `TransactionAmount` column for transactions. The supplier-side table, `Purchasing.SupplierTransactions`, has the same columns, so I could repoint the query there if you meant supplier transactions.

```sql
SELECT AVG(TransactionAmount) AS avg_completed_transaction_amount
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions
WHERE IsFinalized = true;
```

Quantity sold per stock item is best taken from the invoice lines (`Sales.InvoiceLines`), since those represent actual sales. I'll group by stock item and join to `Warehouse.StockItems` for the name. Using a LEFT JOIN from StockItems keeps items with no sales (their average will be NULL).

```sql
SELECT si.StockItemID,
       si.StockItemName,
       AVG(il.Quantity) AS average_quantity_sold
FROM Warehouse.StockItems si
LEFT JOIN Sales.InvoiceLines il ON il.StockItemID = si.StockItemID
GROUP BY si.StockItemID, si.StockItemName
ORDER BY si.StockItemID;
```

The query sums `ExtendedPrice` across invoice lines for invoices dated 1 January to 31 March 2013. I took "revenue" to mean invoiced line totals. `ExtendedPrice` includes tax, so subtract `TaxAmount` if you want revenue excluding tax. I did not run it against the database.

```sql
SELECT SUM(il.ExtendedPrice) AS total_revenue
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines il
JOIN Sales.Invoices i ON i.InvoiceID = il.InvoiceID
WHERE i.InvoiceDate >= DATE '2013-01-01'
  AND i.InvoiceDate < DATE '2013-04-01';
```

Backorders in this schema are represented in Sales.Orders. An order that has a BackorderOrderID points to the backorder created for it. Counting the distinct customers with at least one such order answers the question.

An alternative reading is that a backorder is an order referenced by another order's BackorderOrderID. Both readings identify the same customer, since a backorder is created for the same customer as the original order. So I use the simpler one.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID) AS customers_with_backorders
FROM Sales.Orders
WHERE BackorderOrderID IS NOT NULL;
```

Black Friday 2024 is Friday, 29 November 2024. I treated an order as "with promotion" if any of its lines matches a special deal that was active on the order date. A deal matches when every criterion it specifies (stock item, customer, buying group, customer category, stock group) fits the order line or customer. Order value is the sum of `Quantity * UnitPrice` over the order's lines, before tax.

```sql
WITH order_values AS (
    SELECT o.OrderID,
           SUM(ol.Quantity * ol.UnitPrice) AS order_value,
           BOOL_OR(EXISTS (
               SELECT 1
               FROM Sales.SpecialDeals sd
               WHERE o.OrderDate BETWEEN sd.StartDate AND sd.EndDate
                 AND (sd.StockItemID IS NULL OR sd.StockItemID = ol.StockItemID)
                 AND (sd.CustomerID IS NULL OR sd.CustomerID = o.CustomerID)
                 AND (sd.BuyingGroupID IS NULL OR sd.BuyingGroupID = c.BuyingGroupID)
                 AND (sd.CustomerCategoryID IS NULL OR sd.CustomerCategoryID = c.CustomerCategoryID)
                 AND (sd.StockGroupID IS NULL OR EXISTS (
                         SELECT 1
                         FROM Warehouse.StockItemStockGroups sisg
                         WHERE sisg.StockItemID = ol.StockItemID
                           AND sisg.StockGroupID = sd.StockGroupID))
           )) AS has_promotion
    FROM Sales.Orders o
    JOIN Sales.OrderLines ol ON ol.OrderID = o.OrderID
    JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
    WHERE o.OrderDate = DATE '2024-11-29'
    GROUP BY o.OrderID
)
SELECT CASE WHEN has_promotion THEN 'With promotion' ELSE 'Without promotion' END AS promotion_status,
       COUNT(*) AS order_count,
       ROUND(AVG(order_value), 2) AS average_order_value
FROM order_values
GROUP BY has_promotion
ORDER BY has_promotion DESC;
```

Orders are stored in `Sales.Orders`, and the order date is in the `OrderDate` column, which is a `date` type. So I filter on 2013-11-01 and return all columns.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM Sales.Orders
WHERE OrderDate = DATE '2013-11-01'
ORDER BY OrderID;
```

This query sums `QuantityOnHand` per brand, joining `Warehouse.StockItems` to `Warehouse.StockItemHoldings`, and returns the 10 brands with the most units in stock. I read "stock count" as units on hand rather than the number of distinct stock items. I also excluded items with no brand.

```sql
SELECT si.Brand,
       SUM(sh.QuantityOnHand) AS total_stock_count
FROM Warehouse.StockItems si
JOIN Warehouse.StockItemHoldings sh ON sh.StockItemID = si.StockItemID
WHERE si.Brand IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY si.Brand
ORDER BY total_stock_count DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

Interpretation: a customer "had a backorder" if one of their orders has a `BackorderOrderID` (the order spawned a backorder). I assigned each to a year by `OrderDate`, kept 2000–2020, and counted distinct customers per year. Years with no backorders don't appear in the output.

```sql
SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.OrderDate)::int AS order_year,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.CustomerID) AS customers_with_backorders
FROM Sales.Orders o
WHERE o.BackorderOrderID IS NOT NULL
  AND o.OrderDate >= DATE '2000-01-01'
  AND o.OrderDate < DATE '2021-01-01'
GROUP BY EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.OrderDate)
ORDER BY order_year;
```

Approach: Find the customer who bought the most of the 'Northwind' brand. Join invoice lines to stock items filtered by brand, then to invoices and customers, sum the quantity per customer, and take the top one.

Consumption is measured by quantity purchased. Credit notes would make this less precise, but quantities in invoice lines already reflect the sales, so I'm keeping it simple.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName, SUM(il.Quantity) AS total_quantity
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines il
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
JOIN Sales.Invoices i ON i.InvoiceID = il.InvoiceID
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = i.CustomerID
WHERE si.Brand = 'Northwind'
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
ORDER BY total_quantity DESC
LIMIT 1;
```

Order value = sum of Quantity * UnitPrice over order lines. Compute the value per order first, then average per customer category.

Steps:
1. Calculate each order's total from Sales.OrderLines (Quantity * UnitPrice).
2. Join to Sales.Orders, then Sales.Customers, then Sales.CustomerCategories.
3. Average the order totals per category.

```sql
WITH order_totals AS (
    SELECT o.OrderID,
           o.CustomerID,
           SUM(ol.Quantity * ol.UnitPrice) AS order_value
    FROM Sales.Orders o
    JOIN Sales.OrderLines ol ON ol.OrderID = o.OrderID
    GROUP BY o.OrderID, o.CustomerID
)
SELECT cc.CustomerCategoryName,
       AVG(ot.order_value) AS average_order_value
FROM order_totals ot
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = ot.CustomerID
JOIN Sales.CustomerCategories cc ON cc.CustomerCategoryID = c.CustomerCategoryID
GROUP BY cc.CustomerCategoryName
ORDER BY average_order_value DESC;
```

The question asks for the ratio of salespeople to employees, using the `Application.People` table, which has the `IsSalesperson` and `IsEmployee` flags.

Ambiguity: "employees" could mean people with `IsEmployee = true`. Salespeople in this dataset are also employees, so I'll count salespeople among all employees (those with `IsEmployee = true`) and divide by the total number of employees. To avoid integer division, I'll cast to numeric.

```sql
SELECT
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE IsSalesperson) ::numeric
    / NULLIF(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE IsEmployee), 0) AS salesperson_to_employee_ratio
FROM Application.People;
```

The query assumes delay is the gap between the confirmed delivery time on the invoice and the order's expected delivery date. It joins invoices to orders, then to the customer's delivery city, and averages the delay per city. It returns the five cities with the largest average delay, in days.

```sql
SELECT c.CityName,
       ROUND(AVG(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (i.ConfirmedDeliveryTime - o.ExpectedDeliveryDate::timestamp)) / 86400.0)::numeric, 2) AS avg_delay_days
FROM Sales.Invoices i
JOIN Sales.Orders o ON o.OrderID = i.OrderID
JOIN Sales.Customers cu ON cu.CustomerID = i.CustomerID
JOIN Application.Cities c ON c.CityID = cu.DeliveryCityID
WHERE i.ConfirmedDeliveryTime IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY c.CityID, c.CityName
ORDER BY avg_delay_days DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

The schema has no discount column on orders or invoice lines, so I treated a discounted purchase as an invoice line sold below the stock item's list price. Special deals and standard customer discounts both show up that way. The query counts distinct customers with at least one such line on an invoice dated in 2024. Credit notes are excluded.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT i.CustomerID) AS customers_with_discount_2024
FROM Sales.Invoices i
JOIN Sales.InvoiceLines il ON il.InvoiceID = i.InvoiceID
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
WHERE i.InvoiceDate >= DATE '2024-01-01'
  AND i.InvoiceDate < DATE '2025-01-01'
  AND i.IsCreditNote = false
  AND il.UnitPrice < si.UnitPrice;
```

The question is ambiguous, so I read "how many items they sold" as the total quantity of each supplier's stock items that appear on sales invoice lines.

1. `Sales.InvoiceLines` records each sale, with `StockItemID` and `Quantity`.
2. `Warehouse.StockItems` maps each stock item to its `SupplierID`.
3. `Purchasing.Suppliers` gives the supplier name.
4. I join the three tables, sum `Quantity` per supplier, sort descending and keep the top 5.

```sql
SELECT s.SupplierID,
       s.SupplierName,
       SUM(il.Quantity) AS total_items_sold
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines il
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
JOIN Purchasing.Suppliers s ON s.SupplierID = si.SupplierID
GROUP BY s.SupplierID, s.SupplierName
ORDER BY total_items_sold DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

Stock items live in Warehouse.StockItems, which has both Size and UnitPrice columns. The query groups by Size and averages UnitPrice. Items with a NULL size fall into one group of their own.

```sql
SELECT Size, AVG(UnitPrice) AS average_unit_price
FROM Warehouse.StockItems
GROUP BY Size;
```

The only vehicle data in the schema is `Warehouse.VehicleTemperatures`, which records a `VehicleRegistration` for each reading. Vehicles therefore appear only as distinct registrations, so I count those.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT VehicleRegistration) AS number_of_vehicles
FROM Warehouse.VehicleTemperatures;
```

Two assumptions, since the schema doesn't spell them out:

- **"In stock"** means a row in `Warehouse.StockItemHoldings` with `QuantityOnHand > 0`.
- **"No tax rate attached"** means `TaxRate` in `Warehouse.StockItems` is NULL or 0. The column is declared NOT NULL, so in practice only 0 can match, but checking both is harmless.

I haven't run the query against the data.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS items_in_stock_without_tax_rate
FROM Warehouse.StockItems si
JOIN Warehouse.StockItemHoldings sh ON sh.StockItemID = si.StockItemID
WHERE sh.QuantityOnHand > 0
  AND (si.TaxRate IS NULL OR si.TaxRate = 0);
```

The question is ambiguous. I took "search terms" to mean the `Tags` column on `Warehouse.StockItems`, which holds a JSON array of keywords per item. The query expands each array into individual tags, counts how many stock items carry each tag, and returns the 6 most common. Ties are broken alphabetically. I haven't run it against the database.

```sql
SELECT t.tag AS search_term,
       COUNT(*) AS item_count
FROM Warehouse.StockItems si
CROSS JOIN LATERAL jsonb_array_elements_text(si.Tags::jsonb) AS t(tag)
WHERE si.Tags IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY t.tag
ORDER BY item_count DESC, t.tag
LIMIT 6;
```

Suppliers have a DeliveryCityID that links to Application.Cities. To find the cities with the most suppliers, I'll join the two tables, group by city, count suppliers, and take the top 5. I'm grouping by CityID as well as CityName, since different cities could share a name. Ties are broken by city name so the ordering is deterministic.

```sql
SELECT c.CityName, COUNT(*) AS supplier_count
FROM Purchasing.Suppliers s
JOIN Application.Cities c ON s.DeliveryCityID = c.CityID
GROUP BY c.CityID, c.CityName
ORDER BY supplier_count DESC, c.CityName
LIMIT 5;
```

Reasoning: "Items ordered" means the sum of order line quantities, grouped by order date. I join Sales.Orders to Sales.OrderLines, sum Quantity per OrderDate, and take the top day.

```sql
SELECT o.OrderDate, SUM(ol.Quantity) AS total_items
FROM Sales.Orders o
JOIN Sales.OrderLines ol ON ol.OrderID = o.OrderID
GROUP BY o.OrderDate
ORDER BY total_items DESC
LIMIT 1;
```

The question asks for the ratio of a city's population to the number of suppliers in it, so I'm assuming a supplier's city is its delivery city (`DeliveryCityID`). The query joins suppliers to cities and counts suppliers per city. It then divides the city's `LatestRecordedPopulation` by that count, orders by the ratio from highest to lowest, and keeps the top 5. Cities with no supplier don't appear, which avoids dividing by zero, and cities with no recorded population are excluded.

```sql
SELECT c.CityID,
       c.CityName,
       c.LatestRecordedPopulation,
       COUNT(s.SupplierID) AS supplier_count,
       c.LatestRecordedPopulation::numeric / COUNT(s.SupplierID) AS population_to_supplier_ratio
FROM Application.Cities c
JOIN Purchasing.Suppliers s ON s.DeliveryCityID = c.CityID
WHERE c.LatestRecordedPopulation IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY c.CityID, c.CityName, c.LatestRecordedPopulation
ORDER BY population_to_supplier_ratio DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

The question is ambiguous, so I interpreted "geographical area" as the sales territory and "targets" as where the company's customers are. I joined each customer's delivery city to its state/province, which carries the sales territory, then counted customers per territory and kept the top 3.

```sql
SELECT sp.SalesTerritory,
       COUNT(DISTINCT c.CustomerID) AS customer_count
FROM Sales.Customers c
JOIN Application.Cities ci ON ci.CityID = c.DeliveryCityID
JOIN Application.StateProvinces sp ON sp.StateProvinceID = ci.StateProvinceID
GROUP BY sp.SalesTerritory
ORDER BY customer_count DESC, sp.SalesTerritory
LIMIT 3;
```

Success isn't defined in the schema, so I measured it as total sales revenue (`ExtendedPrice`) from invoice lines that fall under each deal. A line falls under a deal when all of these hold:
- The invoice date is within the deal's start and end dates.
- The stock item matches the deal's item or stock group, if the deal sets one.
- The customer matches the deal's customer, buying group or customer category, if the deal sets one.

I excluded credit notes and returned the top deal by total revenue.

```sql
SELECT sd.SpecialDealID,
       sd.DealDescription,
       SUM(il.ExtendedPrice) AS total_sales,
       SUM(il.Quantity) AS total_quantity,
       COUNT(*) AS line_count
FROM Sales.SpecialDeals sd
JOIN Sales.Invoices i
  ON i.InvoiceDate BETWEEN sd.StartDate AND sd.EndDate
 AND i.IsCreditNote = false
JOIN Sales.Customers c
  ON c.CustomerID = i.CustomerID
JOIN Sales.InvoiceLines il
  ON il.InvoiceID = i.InvoiceID
WHERE (sd.StockItemID IS NULL OR sd.StockItemID = il.StockItemID)
  AND (sd.StockGroupID IS NULL OR EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM Warehouse.StockItemStockGroups sisg
        WHERE sisg.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
          AND sisg.StockGroupID = sd.StockGroupID))
  AND (sd.CustomerID IS NULL OR sd.CustomerID = i.CustomerID)
  AND (sd.BuyingGroupID IS NULL OR sd.BuyingGroupID = c.BuyingGroupID)
  AND (sd.CustomerCategoryID IS NULL OR sd.CustomerCategoryID = c.CustomerCategoryID)
GROUP BY sd.SpecialDealID, sd.DealDescription
ORDER BY total_sales DESC
LIMIT 1;
```

The Continent column in Application.Countries holds "North America", so I filter on it. I trace each invoice line to its country through the customer's delivery city and state/province. I define "best seller" as total quantity sold, so I sum the invoice line quantities per stock item and take the top 4.

```sql
SELECT si.StockItemID,
       si.StockItemName,
       SUM(il.Quantity) AS total_quantity_sold
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines il
JOIN Sales.Invoices i ON i.InvoiceID = il.InvoiceID
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = i.CustomerID
JOIN Application.Cities ci ON ci.CityID = c.DeliveryCityID
JOIN Application.StateProvinces sp ON sp.StateProvinceID = ci.StateProvinceID
JOIN Application.Countries co ON co.CountryID = sp.CountryID
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
WHERE co.Continent = 'North America'
GROUP BY si.StockItemID, si.StockItemName
ORDER BY total_quantity_sold DESC, si.StockItemID
LIMIT 4;
```

This assumes "sale transactions" means rows in `Sales.CustomerTransactions`. The query groups them by calendar month (year and month together) and returns the month with the most rows. I didn't filter by transaction type, so payments and other non-invoice rows are counted too.

```sql
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', TransactionDate)::date AS month,
       COUNT(*) AS transaction_count
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', TransactionDate)
ORDER BY transaction_count DESC
LIMIT 1;
```

Customers who placed more than 130 orders: count rows in Sales.Orders per customer, join to Sales.Customers for the name, and keep those with a count above 130.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName, COUNT(o.OrderID) AS order_count
FROM Sales.Customers c
JOIN Sales.Orders o ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
HAVING COUNT(o.OrderID) > 130
ORDER BY order_count DESC;
```

The question asks for the recorded temperatures in the cold room, with the timestamp and temperature values. The `Warehouse.ColdRoomTemperatures` table holds the readings, with `RecordedWhen` as the timestamp and `Temperature` as the value. I'll select both columns and order by time. The archive table only holds historical versions of rows, so the current table is the right source.

```sql
SELECT RecordedWhen, Temperature
FROM Warehouse.ColdRoomTemperatures
ORDER BY RecordedWhen;
```

Orders link to customers, and customers link to buying groups. To count orders per buying group, I join Orders to Customers and then to BuyingGroups, and group by buying group.

I use an inner join to BuyingGroups, so customers with no buying group are left out. Buying groups that have no orders also won't appear. To list every buying group, including those with zero orders, I would start from BuyingGroups and use left joins instead. The question asks for orders placed by each buying group, so the inner join fits.

```sql
SELECT bg.BuyingGroupID,
       bg.BuyingGroupName,
       COUNT(o.OrderID) AS order_count
FROM Sales.Orders o
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
JOIN Sales.BuyingGroups bg ON c.BuyingGroupID = bg.BuyingGroupID
GROUP BY bg.BuyingGroupID, bg.BuyingGroupName
ORDER BY order_count DESC;
```

Invoices are in Sales.Invoices, and InvoiceDate is a date column. To cover May 2014 I use a half-open range, from 2014-05-01 up to but not including 2014-06-01. That also works if the column later becomes a timestamp.

```sql
SELECT InvoiceID, CustomerID, InvoiceDate
FROM Sales.Invoices
WHERE InvoiceDate >= DATE '2014-05-01'
  AND InvoiceDate < DATE '2014-06-01'
ORDER BY InvoiceDate, InvoiceID;
```

This query totals each supplier's 2014 purchases from `Purchasing.SupplierTransactions`. I counted only "Supplier Invoice" transactions as purchases, so payments and credit notes are excluded. I matched the transaction type by name, and I haven't run it against the data.

```sql
SELECT s.SupplierID,
       s.SupplierName,
       SUM(st.AmountExcludingTax) AS TotalPurchasesExcludingTax,
       SUM(st.TaxAmount)          AS TotalTax,
       SUM(st.TransactionAmount)  AS TotalPurchases
FROM Purchasing.SupplierTransactions st
JOIN Purchasing.Suppliers s ON s.SupplierID = st.SupplierID
JOIN Application.TransactionTypes tt ON tt.TransactionTypeID = st.TransactionTypeID
WHERE tt.TransactionTypeName = 'Supplier Invoice'
  AND st.TransactionDate >= DATE '2014-01-01'
  AND st.TransactionDate < DATE '2015-01-01'
GROUP BY s.SupplierID, s.SupplierName
ORDER BY s.SupplierName;
```

The question asks for a monthly summary, grouped by invoice date, of the total chiller and dry items sold. The Sales.Invoices table holds TotalDryItems and TotalChillerItems, so no joins are needed.

Steps:
1. Truncate InvoiceDate to the month with `DATE_TRUNC('month', InvoiceDate)` to get the monthly grouping.
2. Sum TotalChillerItems and TotalDryItems for each month.
3. Add the two sums to get total items sold.
4. Order by month.

```sql
SELECT
    DATE_TRUNC('month', InvoiceDate)::date AS invoice_month,
    SUM(TotalChillerItems) AS total_chiller_items,
    SUM(TotalDryItems) AS total_dry_items,
    SUM(TotalChillerItems) + SUM(TotalDryItems) AS total_items_sold
FROM Sales.Invoices
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', InvoiceDate)
ORDER BY invoice_month;
```

Order details most naturally means the order lines (items, quantity, price) together with the order header, joined to the customer name.

Steps:
1. Start from Sales.Orders for the order header (OrderID, OrderDate, ExpectedDeliveryDate).
2. Join Sales.Customers on CustomerID to get CustomerName.
3. Join Sales.OrderLines on OrderID to get the line-level details (description, quantity, unit price, tax rate).

```sql
SELECT o.OrderID,
       c.CustomerName,
       o.OrderDate,
       o.ExpectedDeliveryDate,
       ol.OrderLineID,
       ol.StockItemID,
       ol.Description,
       ol.Quantity,
       ol.UnitPrice,
       ol.TaxRate,
       ol.PickedQuantity
FROM Sales.Orders AS o
JOIN Sales.Customers AS c ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
JOIN Sales.OrderLines AS ol ON ol.OrderID = o.OrderID
ORDER BY o.OrderID, ol.OrderLineID;
```

Sales.SpecialDeals holds DealDescription and DiscountAmount, so the total discount per deal description is the sum of DiscountAmount grouped by DealDescription. Rows where DiscountAmount is NULL (percentage-based deals) are ignored by SUM, and a description whose rows are all NULL yields a NULL total.

```sql
SELECT DealDescription,
       SUM(DiscountAmount) AS total_discount_amount
FROM Sales.SpecialDeals
GROUP BY DealDescription
ORDER BY DealDescription;
```

Sales.CustomerTransactions has a TransactionAmount column, which already includes tax (AmountExcludingTax + TaxAmount). Averaging it per customer answers the question. I join to Sales.Customers to show the customer name.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID,
       c.CustomerName,
       AVG(ct.TransactionAmount) AS avg_transaction_amount_including_tax
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions ct
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = ct.CustomerID
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
ORDER BY c.CustomerID;
```

Approach: sum TransactionAmount per customer from Sales.CustomerTransactions, join to Sales.Customers for names, order by the total descending, and limit to 100.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID,
       c.CustomerName,
       SUM(ct.TransactionAmount) AS total_transaction_amount
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions AS ct
JOIN Sales.Customers AS c ON c.CustomerID = ct.CustomerID
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
ORDER BY total_transaction_amount DESC
LIMIT 100;
```

Order details are the rows in Sales.OrderLines, and each row has a StockItemID. Joining that to Warehouse.StockItems on StockItemID gives the stock item name for each line.

```sql
SELECT ol.OrderLineID,
       ol.OrderID,
       ol.StockItemID,
       si.StockItemName,
       ol.Description,
       ol.PackageTypeID,
       ol.Quantity,
       ol.UnitPrice,
       ol.TaxRate,
       ol.PickedQuantity,
       ol.PickingCompletedWhen
FROM Sales.OrderLines AS ol
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems AS si ON si.StockItemID = ol.StockItemID
ORDER BY ol.OrderID, ol.OrderLineID;
```

Join Purchasing.SupplierTransactions to Purchasing.Suppliers on SupplierID to get each transaction along with its supplier's name. An inner join is enough because SupplierID is a NOT NULL foreign key in SupplierTransactions.

```sql
SELECT st.*, s.SupplierName
FROM Purchasing.SupplierTransactions AS st
JOIN Purchasing.Suppliers AS s ON s.SupplierID = st.SupplierID
ORDER BY st.SupplierTransactionID;
```

This query treats an order line as having a special deal when a `Sales.SpecialDeals` row applies to it. A deal applies when the order date falls within the deal's start and end dates. Each criterion the deal sets (stock item, customer, buying group, customer category, stock group) must also match the order line or its customer. A criterion left NULL on the deal is ignored.

```sql
SELECT o.OrderID,
       o.OrderDate,
       o.CustomerID,
       c.CustomerName,
       ol.OrderLineID,
       ol.StockItemID,
       ol.Description,
       ol.Quantity,
       ol.UnitPrice,
       ol.TaxRate,
       sd.SpecialDealID,
       sd.DealDescription,
       sd.StartDate,
       sd.EndDate,
       sd.DiscountAmount,
       sd.DiscountPercentage,
       sd.UnitPrice AS DealUnitPrice
FROM Sales.Orders o
JOIN Sales.OrderLines ol ON ol.OrderID = o.OrderID
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
JOIN Sales.SpecialDeals sd
  ON o.OrderDate BETWEEN sd.StartDate AND sd.EndDate
 AND (sd.StockItemID IS NULL OR sd.StockItemID = ol.StockItemID)
 AND (sd.CustomerID IS NULL OR sd.CustomerID = o.CustomerID)
 AND (sd.BuyingGroupID IS NULL OR sd.BuyingGroupID = c.BuyingGroupID)
 AND (sd.CustomerCategoryID IS NULL OR sd.CustomerCategoryID = c.CustomerCategoryID)
 AND (sd.StockGroupID IS NULL OR EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM Warehouse.StockItemStockGroups sisg
```
